title: Benches clear at Fenway, with Willson Contreras and Cade Cavalli at the center
content:
BOSTON — Boston Red Sox first baseman Willson Contreras was ejected from Tuesday’s Nationals-Red Sox game, following a confrontation with Washington starter Cade Cavalli that cleared the benches at Fenway Park.

With the Red Sox leading 1-0 in the bottom of the fourth on Tuesday night, Cavalli struck out Contreras, who started to walk back to the dugout. Contreras had his head down, but looked up at Cavalli when he heard something.

Contreras, who was also ejected from Monday’s game, began walking toward the mound as Nationals catcher Keibert Ruiz put his hand on Contreras’ shoulder and Red Sox third base coach Chad Epperson approached to intervene. Then came more pushing and shoving, and Contreras charged the mound. He threw his helmet as several players tried to hold him back.

It appeared as though Contreras tried to throw his helmet at Cavalli, but it instead hit Nationals first baseman Andrés Chaparro, who was then enraged. Nationals right-hander Miles Mikolas and Red Sox outfielder Nate Eaton also got into a scuffle on the side of the fray after Mikolas tried to hold back Contreras, a former teammate with the St. Louis Cardinals. After Eaton grabbed Mikolas, the veteran threw Eaton to the grass.

After players retreated to their dugouts, interim manager Chad Tracy met crew chief Vic Carapazza near the Red Sox dugout where the mild-mannered manager grew increasingly incensed before he was thrown out.

Umpires eventually announced Contreras, Eaton and Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy had been ejected. Mikolas was also ejected and tipped his cap to the Fenway crowd on the way out.

It marked the first career ejection for Tracy, who took over in Boston after Alex Cora was fired in late April. It was the 11th ejection of Contreras’ career.

Cavalli was booed when he walked off the field after the inning, when he returned to the mound in the next inning, then again when he made a throw to first — and once more when he threw a sweeper inside to Caleb Durbin. Washington’s Opening Day starter — “our No. 1, our horse,” Nationals manager Blake Butera said after Cavalli’s start last week — had arguably the best outing of his young career, retiring 19 in a row amidst the chaos while striking out 13 in seven innings. It was the most strikeouts by a Nationals pitcher since lefty MacKenzie Gore struck out 13 Rockies last April.

The melee seemed to have some carryover from Monday night, when Contreras hit a three-run homer off Mikolas, throwing his bat with force as he headed to first, then breaking down in tears in the dugout afterward. In the second inning, first base umpire Nick Lentz ejected Contreras for tapping his helmet after a strikeout, which Lentz interpreted as a mocking gesture.

Contreras said after the game that the situation in his home country of Venezuela, where devastating earthquakes have left more than 1,700 people dead, has weighed heavily on his mind, and was the reason for his emotions in the dugout. But he also made a point to say he’d spoken with the Nationals and apologized to Mikolas, noting that he didn’t want to show disrespect to his former Cardinals teammate by throwing his bat after the homer, that it was more a reflection of his distress for family and friends back home.

“I think it’s just the emotional part of Venezuela that got to me, got the best out of me,” Contreras said Monday. “I wasn’t feeling good the whole day, I was kind of down, sad and I hit a homer, of course. I tried to help my dugout, but the first thing that I said was it’s for Venezuela. Of course, I’m helping the team to win, and it’s good, but I think every homer from now on is going to be for the Red Sox and for Venezuela.”

Making matters worse for the Red Sox on Tuesday, starter Connelly Early exited the game with left elbow discomfort. The rookie had thrown four scoreless innings, allowing three hits, but was replaced by Danny Coulombe in the top of the fifth. Early has been a key piece of the rotation for the Red Sox, logging a stretch of 12 straight quality starts, the team’s longest streak since 14 straight in 1988.

This story will be updated.
